E1472.summary: In the Appendix, the place where the originals of the true tools are; outward tools only represent these.
E1472.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says of outward tools “they are representatives of these that are in the Recess of Light” [APP ¶100]. The originals of the true tools are thus placed in the Recess of Light; the text gives no further explanation.

E1473.summary: A collective witness that Plato cites for the saying about the thrysus-bearers.
E1473.body: Plato cites the records of the Mysteries as witness to the saying about the thrysus-bearers [II.4 ¶54].

E1474.summary: A metaphysical birth out of the Infinite into Light, in which the visible springs from the invisible.
E1474.body: Atwood: “the recreation was seen to be a stupendous metaphysical birth out of the Infinite into Light” [III.3 ¶79], in which the visible springs from the invisible.

E1475.summary: The fire within the magic earth that spontaneously binds its parts, coagulates them and stops their flux.
E1475.body: Atwood describes the fire within the magic earth: “this fire binds the parts thereof spontaneously to himself, coagulates them, and stops their flux” [III.2 ¶8]. Arresting the flux of the matter is thus this fire's work.

E1476.summary: The force the alchemists claim man has brought into action through rational conditioning.
E1476.body: A claim Atwood reports for the Alchemists: “man, by rationally conditionating, has succeeded in developing into action the Recreative Force” [II.1 ¶47]. The text does not define the force further.

E1477.summary: The Red, named as the source of the Citrine; its root, the red root, is identified with the Terra Adamica.
E1477.body: Atwood names the Red as the source of the Citrine and asserts an identity: “The red root is the Terra Adamica” [I.3 n52].

E1478.summary: A product of the Work whose process had been laborious and rarely achieved; Basil Valentine reportedly found a new way to work it.
E1478.body: Atwood reports that Basil Valentine found “a new method of working the Red Elixir” [I.1 ¶59]; the process had previously been laborious and rarely achieved. She also cites Norton's lines on the Red Stone as evidence on this point [I.1 ¶60] (see Red Stone).

E1479.summary: In verses from Lucerna Salis Phil., something possessed, together with pure Mercury, by whoever has the vapour of the subject.
E1479.body: In the verses quoted from Lucerna Salis Phil., whoever has the vapour of the subject “Has the gilded splendor of the Red Lyon, The pure and clear Mercury.” [I.2 ¶30]. The text does not explain it further.

E1480.summary: In Eudoxus, one of the two Mercuries, identified with the most sharp Vinegar and called by others the bath of the Sun.
E1480.body: Eudoxus (quoted) speaks of two Mercuries and identifies one: “the most sharp Vinegar is the Red Mercury” [IV.3 ¶10]; he adds that “the Red Mercury is the bath of the Sun” [IV.3 ¶10], a name others give it. Asserted identities: = most sharp Vinegar; = bath of the Sun.

E1481.summary: In Eudoxus, what is struck upon the Stone so that a clear fountain issues from it.
E1481.body: Eudoxus (quoted) directs one to “strike upon it with the Red of Magic Fire” [IV.3 ¶10], whereupon a clear fountain issues from the Stone. The expression is not explained in the text.

E1482.summary: What Kelly is believed to have had, whether by secret information or by making it himself.
E1482.body: Atwood reports the belief that Kelly “became possessed of the Red Powder by some secret kind of information” [I.1 ¶66], or else made it himself. The text does not state outright that it is the same as the Powder of Projection.

E1483.summary: What Ripley tried to putrefy by alternate heat and cold, and which he called his Gold.
E1483.body: The text (voice unclear) says Ripley tried to putrefy “this Red Salt which he enviously calls his Gold” [IV.1 ¶36] by alternate heat and cold. Asserted identity: = Gold (Ripley's name for it).

E1484.summary: The final perfection of the matter, the form of the Stone that turns mercury into gold; also called phoenix, salamander and royal essence.
E1484.body: Nicholas Flamel (quoted) reports: “I made projection of the Red Stone, on a like quantity of mercury” [I.1 ¶57], yielding gold, where the earlier projection had yielded silver. Norton (quoted) says scarcely one in fifteen kingdoms possesses it — “In fifteen kingdoms hath our Red Stone.” — that it is not to be sought until the white medicine is fully wrought, and that it can be increased in multiplication; the passage also has the form “Had not of our Res Stone consideration” [I.1 ¶60]. Atwood cites these lines as evidence about the Red Elixir. In her own voice the Red Stone is the final perfection of the matter: “it is henceforth a phoenix, salamander, their royal essence and Red Stone” [I.2 ¶40]. Asserted identities: = phoenix; = salamander; = royal essence.

E1485.summary: In verses from Lucerna Salis Phil., the red Sulfur contained in the subject, knowledge of which gives the whole foundation.
E1485.body: From the verses quoted from Lucerna Salis Phil.: “And he who knows the red Sulfur which it contains, Has within his power the whole foundation” [I.2 ¶30]. The text does not explain it further.

E1486.summary: In Hermes, a redness corrupted with water, held like fire in a live coal, to be purified by repeated withdrawal; called the soul.
E1486.body: Hermes (quoted) instructs: “Take, my Son, this redness, corrupted with the water” [I.3 ¶17]; it holds its fire like a live coal and is to be purified by repeated withdrawal. A note identifies it: “the redness is its soul” [I.3 n21], the soul of the passive spirit. Asserted identity: = soul.

E1487.summary: In the Appendix, what brings the philosophical dissolution to an end.
E1487.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says of the philosophical dissolution that “this continues until the refixation takes place” [APP ¶96].

E1488.summary: Exclaimed over as a most mighty and surpassing magic, right after the account of life's return to its source; not defined.
E1488.body: Atwood exclaims “Most mighty and surpassing magic of Reflection.” [III.3 ¶79], directly after describing life's return to its source. The term is not defined there.

E1489.summary: The inferior nature, i.e. the person engaged in the rite, from whom divine things do not take their principle of energy.
E1489.body: The text (voice unclear) glosses the term itself: divine things do not take their principle of energy “from an inferior nature (i.e., to say, from the regardant subject)” [II.4 ¶31]. The regardant subject is the one engaged in the rite. Asserted identity: = inferior nature.

E1490.summary: In the Appendix, the life that begins when the individual mind contacts universal power, ferments the sensorium of this life and lives on its decease.
E1490.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says the contact of the individual mind with power universal is its start: “that experience is the initial of the regenerate life” [APP ¶175]. This life ferments the sensorium of the present life and lives upon its decease. See regeneration.

E1491.summary: The soul that puts on the Stone as a new body.
E1491.body: Atwood says the Stone is what “the regenerate soul puts on as a new body” [IV.4 ¶20]. See regeneration.

E1492.summary: In the Moorish philosopher, the wisdom of a man reformed into God's image, by which he possesses all things and unlocks nature's mysteries.
E1492.body: The Moorish philosopher (quoted) says the man reformed into God's image “in his regenerate Wisdom possesseth all things, and with this light can unlock the most hidden and recluse mysteries of nature” [II.1 ¶9].

E1493.summary: The recreative process, physical and spiritual, by which the vital principle is reconstructed, the natural life dissolved and the Identity made; the process the Hermetic Art serves.
E1493.body:
Atwood's term for the process the Art serves. Already in Part I she says the Poimander and Asclepian books “denote rather our divine capabilities and promise of regeneration than the physical ground of either” [I.1 ¶7], that physical ground being treated with the practical method in the Tractatus Aureus; and in early Christianity “the mystery of human regeneration, so zealously proclaimed, was also rationally understood” [I.1 ¶11]. Only by it can an immortal essence “pass into immortality” [II.4 ¶7].

As process: it is the miraculous principle “by which the relationships of the vital elements are exchanged” [III.1 ¶50] — the sensible medium becomes occult and the occult, catholic reason of life becomes manifest. In it is made “that Identity which is made in the regeneration” [III.2 ¶16], by reprocedure into experience out of an artificially induced dissolute void of life. Upon dissolution of the natural life, “in the regeneration this Reason is said to be discovered” [III.3 ¶52], arising through self-perceivance; the Stone is made manifest regeneratively. It is the physical secret the Mysteries refer to; its first principle: “The first, I the regeneration, is the Word of God independent without all human will” [III.3 ¶77]. It is renewal by Water and the Spirit; “baptismal regeneration was an effectual rite” [IV.2 ¶17], and Christ is brought forth anew as “the seed of his own regeneration” [IV.2 ¶18]. With the fall it is “the ancient doctrine” [IV.3 ¶38], understood only through self-knowledge.

The Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) adds: the vital principle is reconstructed “through a regeneration” [APP ¶68] in “the recreative process of the regeneration” [APP ¶55], the macrocosm's image being evolved before the mental eye; the Hermetically regenerated give up the head life. It brings the whole of life into the Sonship: “It is the death to sin with a new birth awakened in us” [APP ¶79]; begun by the pure earth, it is highest when the spirit, dead to its identity, re-arises as the Divine image — “the condition of the highest regeneration” [APP ¶87]. The philosophic birth “is known in Regeneration, individually proven and proving all” [APP ¶108]; regenerate bodies are penetrated with Light, and the regenerate soul receives body from the residuum of the sensual medium. “The mystery is an art revealed to regenerating men, to advance them on to perfection” [APP ¶146]; it gives freedom to realize every volition, later surrendered to the Father's Will, and involves “a drawing of power and life up through the feet” [APP ¶158].

E1494.summary: In the Author of the Open Entrance, the succession of colours the matter passes through, run through again in each multiplication.
E1494.body: The Author of the Open Entrance (quoted) says that in multiplication “every regiment of the colors will in that brief space be passed through” [IV.3 ¶18]: the whole succession of colours recurs, but quickly.

E1495.summary: In the Appendix, the wise men's name for the analogical sphere, of only relative truth, valued by Hermetists only for its derived light stripped of phantasmagoric form.
E1495.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood: “There is a certain truth in the analogical sphere, but it is only relative. The wise called it the Regio phantastica” [APP ¶105]. For the Hermetists “it was as a pabalum for them, but only when deprived of all phantasmagoric form” [APP ¶105] — valued for the derived light of its essence. Some visionaries “misconceive this Evester, as Paracelsus calls it” [APP ¶105]. Asserted identities: = the analogical sphere; = Evester (Paracelsus's name).

E1496.summary: The religion whose pursuit was punished by death once the Mysteries were abandoned, as the Asclepian prophecy foretold.
E1496.body: The Asclepian Dialogue of Hermes (quoted) prophesies that in a degenerate age “a capital punishment shall be appointed for him who applies himself to the Religion of Intellect” [I.1 ¶10]. Atwood takes up the phrase, in quotation marks, for the time when the Mysteries were abandoned and Theurgic rites proscribed: “a punishment, no less than death, was menaced against him who dared to pursue the "Religion of Intellect"” [I.1 ¶30]; then “tradition and secular delirium had taken place of intellectual enthusiasm, and idle dreams were set up as oracles in the place of Divine inspiration” [I.1 ¶30]. The term is not further defined.

E1497.summary: The soul's recovery of what it forgot in embodied life — the awakened recollection of the intellect that the rites produce, sought by Reason in her root of Light.
E1497.body: Atwood: the soul “will recollect all those things, the remembrance of which she loses in the present life” [II.1 ¶50]; souls allied to antecedent realities feel it, “thrilling into reminiscence, as of some long past life forgotten” [II.1 ¶53]; it is also the recovery of the ancient experiment. The rites work by “awakening intellect into reminiscence” [II.4 ¶36], but the hidden Reason cannot “be awakened to reminiscence without a resolution of the whole circulatory confine” [II.4 ¶39]. Reason, roused from lethargy, goes “to seek for genuine reminiscence in her root of Light” [IV.4 ¶15].

E1498.summary: Author of The Mirific Word and De Arte Cabalistica, whom Atwood cites approvingly for the purified principle, Wisdom as darkness turned to light, and the mirific Word's two natures.
E1498.body: Atwood lists John Reuchlin among those who blended alchemy and therapeutics with neoplatonism and cabala [I.1 ¶39]. From The Mirific Word she takes support for the purified principle as medium of divine experience: “Ex natura et divino factum est” [II.2 ¶25] (ours: 'it is made from nature and the divine'; the book's own rendering is not in the packet). From De Arte Cabalistica, third book: “Nihil est in principio nisi Sapientia.” [III.2 ¶10] (ours: 'there is nothing in the beginning but Wisdom'), with Wisdom as Ain in darkness and the dark Aleph turned to light Aleph. From de Verbo Mirificao: two natures in the mirific Word, the changeable and the immutable — “the other nature or principiating substance is incorruptible, immutable, and always subsistent” [III.2 ¶24; III.2 n25] — which is said to allude to arresting the flux. She uses him throughout as supporting authority.

E1499.summary: The Book of Revelation, which Atwood cites for the competent minister, the Stone with a new name, the white splendour, Wisdom's fruits and the marriage of man and God.
E1499.body: Atwood cites Revel. 3:7 for the qualifications of the competent minister: “he that hath the Key of David, he that openeth, and no man shutteth” [IV.3 ¶39; IV.3 n17]. Chapters 2–3 support the promises of material fruits with Wisdom: “To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the Tree of Life” [IV.3 n22]; the passages at [IV.3 ¶41–45] apparently come from these chapters (the footnote numbering is unclear). Chapters 1:14 and 2:17 illustrate the white appearance of the primeval splendour (the White Stone, the Son of Man): “whose hair was like wool, and white as snow” [III.2 ¶4; III.2 n5]. She also invokes the Stone of the Apocalypse and the Stone with the new name [II.3 ¶52, ¶54]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) the Book of Revelation is said to hint at the marriage-union between man and God in Christ [APP ¶79].

E1500.summary: In Kirchringius, the sudden arrival of a solution after persistent desire and labour, given only to one who prays with great desire and labour.
E1500.body: Kirchringius (quoted): after persistent prayer, desire and labour, “at length, in a moment, the solution will fall in; this is a revelation” [III.4 ¶22]. Asserted identity: = the solution falling in.

forms: Revelations, Open Entrances, New Lights and True Lights, Sunshine and Moonshine, Auroras, Dawns, Manuals, Introductory Lexicons, Triumphal Chariots, Banners, Gates, Keys, Guides
E1501.summary: Atwood's list of generic alchemical book titles, all pointing to the Royal Road once it is found but useless to most modern readers.
E1501.body: Atwood lists these generic titles of alchemical books — Revelations, Open Entrances, New Lights and True Lights, Sunshine and Moonshine, Auroras, Dawns, Manuals, Introductory Lexicons, Triumphal Chariots, Banners, Gates, Keys, Guides — to show that all direct to the Royal Road once it is found, yet are useless to most modern readers [III.4 ¶15].
